---
title: "Packs & configuration"
description: "Use the packs you have, ship your own in a Claude plugin, and tune hook settings."
aliases: [plugin-packs.html, configuration.html]
---

Packs bundle hooks you install once and get everywhere. Exactly two providers exist — the capt-hook wheel's builtins and Claude Code plugins — with zero per-repo config: no manifest, no enable list, no `.claude/capt-hook.toml`. This page covers using the packs you have, shipping your own in a plugin, and tuning hook settings.

## Builtin packs activate themselves

`capt-hook` ships seven builtin packs. Five are always active in every repo:

- `general` — language-agnostic guards: git/jj command safety, a session guard that denies
  `pkill`/`killall`, a `kill` or `renice` of a pid unless this session can prove it
  started the process, since ancestry alone does not establish ownership,
  the harness's `TaskStop` tool from a subagent or Orca lane, since a bare task id does not tell a
  disposable shell task from a workflow, agent, or teammate session (the root session stops any
  of its tasks unchecked),
  `orca terminal close`/`worktree rm`/`worker-stop` (the root coordinating a dispatch's Orca Run may
  stop that dispatch with one literal `worker-stop`), `launchctl` teardown, session-ending
  `osascript`/`softwareupdate`/`pmset`/`tmux`, and `shutdown`/`reboot`, in Bash and in MCP payloads,
  doc and prompt nudges, task and plan discipline, model-routing nudges, a code-review gate, a
  docs-freshness gate, a detour
  check-in nudge, a tooling nudge that asks for a tool-fix lane after a first-party tool refuses, a
  manual workaround next to a tool, or a command repeated by hand, verbose-comment enforcement (a new over-budget comment is denied; an edit to a
  comment that was already over budget only warns), `rm` safety, and a plain-English reply rewrite.
  An owner ruling lifts a terminal close, launchd service stop, or a lane's `TaskStop` through
  [grants](grants.qmd#lift-a-session-guard-block), with one use per ruling and scope across
  all session trees and a two-minute window for identical retries. A lifted Bash call must
  run once at top level, first in the payload, with only pipe successors. A session may
  also close an idle Orca terminal it proves it created itself.
  The rewrite sends each assistant reply through Cerebras (`qwen-3.8-27b`) and does nothing until
  `CEREBRAS_API_KEY` is set. With the key set, it hides the reply's streamed chunks and shows the
  rewrite in their place once the last chunk arrives. Code blocks, names, numbers, and commands carry
  over unchanged. A reply with under 200 characters of prose outside code blocks shows as written, and
  a failed or empty rewrite shows the original reply and records a fault.
- `fixes` — workarounds for upstream Claude Code issues: auto-approving a teammate's permission
  dialogs and scratch-file writes when the session ran with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.
- `steering` — judgment nudges: prefer first-principles fixes over band-aids, don't dismiss a real
  pre-existing issue, don't chase trivial type noise, don't swap the requested fix for docs.
- `performance` — wall-clock pipelining nudges that speculate a held fix while verification runs, plus a
  subprocess resource monitor. One host ticker in `capt-hookd` samples the children of each registered
  session. When a child runs past `min_runtime_seconds` at sustained CPU or disk pressure, the monitor warns
  the session through its next hook event and a desktop notification, then waits out the grace period.
  It then asks the small-tier judge whether the child is disposable. If the judge says yes, the monitor sends
  one targeted `SIGTERM` after it revalidates the pid, parent, process group, start time, command, working
  directory, and session ownership. Deploys, releases, publishes, database clients and migrators, and
  anything protected are never signaled, and neither are their ancestors. Protected means agent sessions,
  terminal hosts, PTY daemons, Orca, launchd, and the Captain Hook host. The judge cannot override those
  exclusions. See [Tune the subprocess resource monitor](#tune-the-subprocess-resource-monitor) to
  change the thresholds or turn the monitor off.
- `graphite` — Graphite (gt) workflow guards that stay inert outside a `gt repo init`'d repo.
  Every hook checks for `.git/.graphite_repo_config` across worktrees and honors `ccx.nogt`.
  That git-config key opts a repo out of the gt lane, so a stale marker cannot activate the pack.
  Neither can a marker on a repo Graphite has no access to: with ccx on PATH the pack reads
  `ccx vcs lane --json` and stands down wherever ccx reports a lane other than `gt`, five-minute
  cached per repository so a linked worktree and its main checkout read one verdict.
  One hook refuses a command; the rest note or rewrite. A jj write gets a note saying the repository's stack lives in
  Graphite; read-only `jj` commands (`log`, `status`, `diff`, `bookmark list`, …) get none when
  *every* `jj` call on the line is a read. Raw `git commit`/`git push`/branch writes get a note
  naming `ccx vcs ship`/`ccx vcs stack new`. Its presubmit review reminder quiets once a cc-review
  pass has run or the session's dispatch prompt contains a whole `ccx: role=fix` line. Any
  `role` value counts because the parent owns the lane's review pass. Rebase, merge, and
  pull notes name `ccx vcs stack rebase` (ccx 0.65.0 or later) or
  `ccx vcs stack submit`. When ccx is on PATH, a stack write with a ccx twin is rewritten to it:
  `gt submit`, `gt s`, and `gt ss` become `ccx vcs stack submit` (`-d`/`--draft` carries over as
  `--draft`), and a bare `gt restack` becomes `ccx vcs stack restack`. A `git push --force-with-lease` of the checked-out branch to `origin`, with no
  lease value of its own, becomes `ccx vcs push`, which force-pushes under a lease only when the
  branch was rewritten and refuses a remote head the branch never held. The rewrite applies only when the ccx verb covers every flag on the call and no
  wrapper, env prefix, or global option would be dropped. Everything else it routes, from
  `gt sync`, `gt create`, `gt modify`, a scoped `gt restack`, and `git rebase` to a plain
  `git push --force`, runs as written with a note naming the ccx command. A rebase control
  (`--continue`, `--abort`, `--skip`) inside a ccx conflict workspace runs as written too, with a note
  naming `ccx vcs stack continue` / `abort` (ccx 0.65.0 or later), since it is the workaround when
  that verb fails. End a command with a real shell comment, `# ccx:raw`, or set
  `CAPT_HOOK_CCX_RAW=1` for the session, to run it as written and silence the note. Quoted
  text and heredoc bodies do not count as comments. Only `1`, `true`, or `yes` enable the
  environment escape. Matching ignores case and surrounding whitespace; `0` does not count. With ccx
  on PATH, a `gh pr view --json` query for landing fields warns and names `ccx vcs pr status <n>`
  (ccx 0.64.1 or later) or `ccx vcs status`; the warning quiets after either command runs this
  session. The one refusal is a push to a PR the Graphite merge queue holds. With ccx on PATH,
  `git push`, `ccx vcs push`, `ccx vcs ship`, `ccx vcs stack submit`, and `gt submit` look up
  each pushed branch's open PR and read their queue state in one `ccx vcs pr status --json` call.
  A queued PR that receives any head but the commit the queue admitted is refused. The queue
  lands that commit and drops the rest, so the refusal names `ccx vcs stack new <name>` and
  `ccx vcs ship` to put the change in a stacked PR instead. When the queued PR is only a parent
  that a `ccx vcs ship` would push along with its downstack, the refusal names
  `ccx vcs ship --tip-only` instead, which pushes only the shipped branch. `# ccx:raw` or
  `CAPT_HOOK_CCX_RAW=1` pushes anyway, and a lookup that fails or times out allows the push.

Two more activate by language, detected from the repo's build manifests:

- `go` — a go-test-before-commit gate and a `go.mod` nudge — active when a recursive, non-ignored
  `go.mod` or `go.work` exists anywhere in the repo.
- `python` — a pytest-before-commit gate, AST style rules, and a `uv` missing-dependency nudge —
  active when a recursive, non-ignored `pyproject.toml` exists.

Detection walks the repo once, pruning VCS metadata and `.gitignore`d directories, so a vendored
`go.mod` under `.venv` or a testdata `pyproject.toml` you ignore never counts. There is no opt-out for
a builtin: to change what fires, fix the policy in `capt-hook` itself rather than adding a repo
exception. To turn every capt-hook behavior off, disable the captain-hook plugin — its wiring dispatches every event, so without it no hook runs, builtin or plugin.

## List the active packs

`pack list` shows the active builtins plus any pack your enabled plugins ship — read-only, no config
to edit:

```bash
uvx capt-hook pack list
```

```
  builtin:fixes                      builtin  2 hooks
  builtin:general                    builtin  13 hooks
  builtin:graphite                   builtin  1 hooks
  builtin:performance                builtin  3 hooks
  builtin:python                     builtin  3 hooks
  builtin:steering                   builtin  3 hooks
  plugin:cc-context@cc-context       plugin   32 hooks
  # ...plus a row per pack your other enabled plugins ship
```

A pack's runtime id is `builtin:<name>` for a wheel builtin and `plugin:<plugin-id>` for a plugin
pack. A plugin pack's version, description, and repository all derive from its `plugin.json` — nothing
about a pack is separately authored.

## Test your own hooks

`capt-hook test` runs the inline tests on your repo's own `.claude/hooks/` modules:

```bash
uvx capt-hook test
```

The builtins are tested by captain-hook itself, and a plugin's pack is tested from its own repo with
[`pack test`](#test-the-pack) — so `capt-hook test` covers only what your repo owns.

## How packs combine with your own hooks

Your `.claude/hooks/` modules import first, so they register ahead of every pack. A block from any hook
wins the event outright; among approvals the first registered wins, so a local approval outranks a
pack's on the same event. Packs are the shared baseline; your local hooks stay authoritative.

## Author a pack

A pack is a directory of hook `.py` files plus an optional `pack.toml` descriptor. Each hook file is a
flat module that imports from `captain_hook` and registers with the same primitives you use locally:

```python
from captain_hook import Allow, Block, Input, block_command

block_command(
    ["git", "push", "--force"],
    reason="Force-push rewrites shared history",
    hint="Push a new commit instead",
    tests={
        Input(command="git push --force"): Block(),
        Input(command="git push"): Allow(),
    },
)
```

You ship that pack to other repos by putting it inside a Claude plugin at the fixed path
`capt-hook/{pack.toml, hooks/}`. [Ship a pack in a plugin](#ship-a-pack-in-a-plugin) covers the layout,
the descriptor, and the `pack test` authoring lane end to end.

## Ship a pack in a plugin

A Claude plugin can carry one capt-hook pack, and dispatch discovers it: every event, the dispatcher
enumerates the project's enabled plugins and loads the pack any of them ships at the fixed path
`capt-hook/{pack.toml, hooks/}` under the plugin root. The pack applies to whatever project the plugin
is enabled in, with zero repo edits and zero per-session wiring — the plugin runs nothing itself.

There is no other way to distribute a pack: no GitHub sources, no tarballs, no pins, no per-repo enable
list. A standalone pack becomes a minimal plugin.

### The layout

A pack plugin ships its pack at one fixed path:

```text
your-plugin/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
└── capt-hook/
    ├── pack.toml
    └── hooks/
        ├── guard.py
        └── ...
```

The `capt-hook/` directory is the pack. Present, it must carry both a `pack.toml` and a `hooks/`
directory; a `capt-hook/` missing either, or with a malformed `pack.toml`, is a **fatal** load error at
every dispatch in every repo that enables the plugin — never a silent skip, because a dropped pack
silently drops guards. A plugin with no `capt-hook/` directory merely consumes packs and is skipped.
Wire `pack test` (below) into the plugin's CI so a malformed pack is caught before release.

### `pack.toml` is a tiny descriptor

The descriptor holds only what can't be derived from the plugin — its identity, version, description,
and repository all come from `plugin.json`. So `pack.toml` carries just two things, both optional:

```toml
# Resources the pack's hooks need provisioned before they run.
resources = ["spacy:en_core_web_sm", "wordnet:oewn:2025"]

# MCP tool gate semantics: how a tool lowers to a built-in gate.
[tools.ccx_code_edit]
behaves_like = "Edit"
span_edit = { path = "path", content = "content", delete = "delete" }

[tools.BashFormat]
behaves_like = "Bash"
```

`resources` names NLP or tool resources the pack's hooks need eagerly provisioned; `capt-hook`
provisions the union of every active pack's resources once at session start. A `[tools.<name>]` table
tells `capt-hook` an MCP tool behaves like a built-in gate — its key is the **bare tool segment**
(`ccx_code_edit`, not `mcp__server__ccx_code_edit`), which matches the tool under any server or mount
prefix. A tool name may be claimed by only one pack; a collision across packs is fatal. A pack that
needs neither still ships a `pack.toml` (an empty `resources = []` is fine) — the file is what declares
`capt-hook/` an intentional pack.

### The captain-hook dependency

`plugin.json` must declare the captain-hook dependency with a version floor:

```json
{
  "dependencies": [
    { "name": "captain-hook", "marketplace": "captain-hook", "version": ">=11.0.0" }
  ]
}
```

The object form is required: `name`, `marketplace`, and a `>=X.Y.Z` floor. This dependency is what
pulls the dispatcher onto a machine that installs only your plugin; without it the pack has no runtime.

### Test the pack {#test-the-pack}

`pack test` validates and runs a working-tree pack, so CI needs one line:

```bash
uvx capt-hook pack test .
```

Pass the plugin root — the directory holding `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` and `capt-hook/`. It requires
all three artifacts, validates the captain-hook dependency floor, validates the `pack.toml` resources
and tool specs, loads only this working-tree pack, and runs its inline tests. It exits non-zero on a
missing layout, a bad dependency, an unknown resource, a load error, zero hooks, an `async_=True`
decision hook, or a failing test.

### Tell users how to install

Two lines — your marketplace and your plugin:

```bash
claude plugin marketplace add your-org/your-repo
claude plugin install your-plugin@your-marketplace
```

On a machine that has never seen captain-hook, installing just your plugin surfaces Claude Code's
dependency error: the `plugin.json` dependency points at a marketplace the machine doesn't know, so the
plugin lands disabled with `dependency-unsatisfied`. The one-time fix is registering the marketplace —
`claude plugin marketplace add yasyf/captain-hook`, or `capt-hook init` in any repo, which registers it
as a side effect. From then on the dependency resolves and Claude Code installs the dispatcher itself.

### How discovery works

Dispatch reads the project's plugin roster from Claude Code's own files on every discovery, with no
subprocess. `~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json` lists each install's path, scope, and, for a
project or local install, the project it belongs to. The `enabledPlugins` maps in the user, project,
local, and managed settings files decide which plugins are on, with the higher-precedence file
winning. In a git worktree the local settings file is the one at the main checkout's root, as in
Claude Code. Discovery then checks each enabled install's root for the fixed `capt-hook/` path. Installing,
enabling, or disabling a plugin takes effect on the next event, and so does editing a hook file inside
a plugin.

A plugin can be installed at more than one scope. Discovery ignores installs that belong to another
project, skips install paths that no longer exist, and follows Claude Code's precedence among the rest:
local over project over user. Two different install paths at the same scope of one project mean a
corrupt roster, and so does an `installed_plugins.json` that isn't a roster object. Either way
discovery loads zero plugin packs and records the error where `capt-hook status` and the next session
start show it.

Policy that arrives outside these files, such as an MDM plist, a remote managed policy, or per-session
flags like `--plugin-dir` and `--settings`, is not visible to discovery.

Discovered packs are first-class: they show in `uvx capt-hook pack list` as kind `plugin`. Their inline
tests run from the plugin's own repo with `pack test`, not from a consuming project's `capt-hook test`.

### Route a misfire home

When the session reviewer mines a misfiring hook, it routes the fix PR to the pack's home repo: a
builtin pack's fix goes to captain-hook, and a plugin pack's fix goes to the `repository` in its
`plugin.json`. A plugin that declares no `repository` has no route, so its misfires are dropped rather
than misfiled.

## Configure hook settings

You define a
`HooksSettings` subclass in `.claude/hooks/conf.py`, override its fields from
code or environment variables, and read the values inside a handler through
`evt.ctx.c`.

### Define a settings class

Create `.claude/hooks/conf.py` and subclass `HooksSettings`. Add your own
fields with type annotations and defaults:

```python
from captain_hook import HooksSettings


class ProjectSettings(HooksSettings):
    test_command: str = "pytest"
    require_tests_after_edit: bool = True
```

The loader discovers `conf.py` when it imports your hooks package, finds the
`HooksSettings` subclass, and instantiates it for every event. You do not call
any builder yourself. Put exactly one subclass in `conf.py` so the loader has a
single class to pick.

### Read settings in a handler

Every event carries the active settings on `evt.ctx.c`. Cast it to your
subclass to get typed field access:

```python
from typing import cast

from captain_hook import Event, Tool, on

from .conf import ProjectSettings


@on(Event.PreToolUse, only_if=[Tool("Bash")])
def enforce_test_command(evt):
    settings = cast(ProjectSettings, evt.ctx.c)
    if (cmd := evt.command).raw and cmd.q.runs("pytest") and settings.test_command != "pytest":
        return evt.block(f"Run the project test command: {settings.test_command}")
    return None
```

### Override fields from the environment

`HooksSettings` reads environment variables with the `HOOKS_` prefix, so each
field maps to one variable. Set `HOOKS_TEST_COMMAND=mtest` to override
`test_command` without touching `conf.py`. List and tuple fields take JSON:

```bash
HOOKS_PLANNING_AGENTS='["Explore","Plan","research"]'
```

To namespace project settings under a different prefix, set `model_config` on
your subclass:

```python
from pydantic_settings import SettingsConfigDict

from captain_hook import HooksSettings


class ProjectSettings(HooksSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_prefix="MYAPP_")
    require_tests_after_edit: bool = True
```

Now `MYAPP_REQUIRE_TESTS_AFTER_EDIT=false` flips the field, and every inherited
field moves under the new prefix too. Pick the prefix once at the project root
and keep it stable.

### Tune the built-in fields

`HooksSettings` ships built-in fields you can override the same way.

#### `planning_agents`

A list of subagent names that the framework treats as scratch work, not real
edits. `skip_planning_agents` is on by default for every hook, so hooks ignore
`Event.SubagentStart` and `Event.SubagentStop` for any agent on this list and
planning runs do not trip your gates. The defaults cover Claude Code's built-in
planning agents, such as `Explore` and `Plan`. Add your own when your team uses
custom planning agent types:

```python
class ProjectSettings(HooksSettings):
    planning_agents: list[str] = [
        *HooksSettings.model_fields["planning_agents"].default_factory(),
        "research",
    ]
```

#### `waiting_tools`

A list of tool names that mean the agent is waiting on something external, not
working. The `Waiting()` condition reads this list to suppress nudges and
gates while a background tool is still running. The defaults cover Claude
Code's long-running tools, such as `Monitor` and `TeamCreate`. Append
your custom async tools to the defaults:

```python
class ProjectSettings(HooksSettings):
    waiting_tools: list[str] = [
        *HooksSettings.model_fields["waiting_tools"].default_factory(),
        "MyAsyncTask",
    ]
```

#### `state_dir`

Where `@session_state` and `@workflow_state` models persist their JSON. The
field reads `CAPTAIN_HOOK_STATE_DIR`, falling back to `~/.claude/state`. Set
`CAPTAIN_HOOK_STATE_DIR` to relocate state, which helps in CI sandboxes that
block writes outside the workspace. See [State and sessions](state.qmd) for how
state directories are laid out.

#### `log_dir`

Where the framework writes its own session logs. The field reads
`CAPTAIN_HOOK_LOG_DIR` and otherwise falls back to `~/.cache/captain-hook/logs`,
or to `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/captain-hook/logs` when you set `XDG_CACHE_HOME`.

### Tune the subprocess resource monitor {#tune-the-subprocess-resource-monitor}

The `performance` pack's resource monitor reads `PerformanceSettings`, which uses the
`HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_` prefix. The defaults live in `internal/wireproto/resource.json`, so the
Go host and the Python worker read one set of numbers.

The host reads the first ten keys below and the worker reads all fourteen. Where each value comes from
differs by key:

- **Per session:** the host takes the thresholds, the grace period, the escalation delay, and the per-session
  cap from the environment of the request that registers the session. Set those in the shell that launches
  Claude Code.
- **Per daemon:** the sample interval and the registry cap come from the environment `capt-hookd` started
  with. The interval also sets how many samples fill the sustain window. A session's own
  `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_SECONDS` does not change either one.
- **Worker:** the worker reads its keys from the environment of each hook run, so they follow the session.

| Key | Default | Valid range | Read by | Meaning |
|-----|---------|-------------|---------|---------|
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_ENABLED` | `true` | `true` or `false` | host and worker | Turns the monitor on or off |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_SAMPLE_INTERVAL_SECONDS` | `15` | 1 to 86400 | host, daemon | Seconds between ticks of the shared sampler |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_MIN_RUNTIME_SECONDS` | `120` | 1 to 86400 | host | A child must have run this long before it can raise pressure |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_CPU_FRACTION` | `0.5` | above 0, up to 1 | host | CPU use that counts as heavy, as a fraction of one core |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_SUSTAIN_SECONDS` | `60` | 1 to 86400 | host | How long CPU or disk use must stay heavy before the warning |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_DISK_BYTES_PER_SECOND` | `52428800` | 0 or more | host | Disk throughput that counts as heavy, 50 `MiB` per second |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_GRACE_SECONDS` | `60` | 1 to 86400 | host | Wait between the warning and the judge |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_ESCALATE_AFTER_SECONDS` | `30` | 0 to 86400 | host | Wait after `SIGTERM` before the escalation stage; `0` disables escalation |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_MAX_TRACKED_PER_SESSION` | `32` | 1 or more | host | Children tracked at once per session |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_REGISTRY_CAP` | `512` | 1 or more | host, daemon | Sessions the host monitors at once |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_TERMINATE` | `true` | `true` or `false` | worker | Whether a disposable verdict ends in a signal |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_JUDGE_TIER` | `small` | a model tier | worker | Model tier that rates whether a child is disposable |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `20` | 1 to 300 | worker | Time limit for one judge call |
| `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_MAX_JUDGE_CALLS_PER_SESSION` | `10` | 1 or more | worker | Judge calls allowed per session |

An invalid value does not stop the session. If the daemon's own environment holds one, the daemon logs the
error and runs with the defaults. If a session's environment holds one, the host logs the error and does
not monitor that session. In the worker, an invalid value makes the stage refuse.

To keep the warnings and never stop a process, set termination off:

```bash
export HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_TERMINATE=false
```

The warning then says termination is off, and the judge stage leaves the child running. To switch the
monitor off entirely, set `HOOKS_PERFORMANCE_ENABLED=false`.

#### What stops a signal

The monitor signals a child only when every check passes. Each of these conditions leaves the process
running instead:

- The stage has no current qualifying reading, or the process table, the child's row, or the child's working
  directory is unreadable. A child with no readable working directory is never signaled, and a child whose
  current readings are all unknown is not signaled at any stage, escalation included.
- A sample that cannot be read empties the window for that metric. Pressure must then be proven again with
  fresh readable samples before the child advances.
- The command line, or an ancestor's, matches an exclusion, or the child or one of its ancestors is protected.
- The judge times out, returns invalid output, has no backend, runs out of its per-session calls, or does not
  rate the child disposable.
- The event payload is malformed, or the session state on disk is corrupt.
- The host cannot dispatch the stage: it is shed, it expired or was abandoned past its deadline, or the host is closing.
- The registry is full, or the session's settings are invalid, so the session is never monitored.

Only the warn stage waits for an acknowledgment. The warn hook answers proceed, and the host stops
tracking the child when the answer is anything else. The judge and escalate stages are fire and forget from the
host's side: the host does not read the reply. Every refusal in the worker records a notice that the next
hook event delivers to the session instead.

The host also refuses a `ResourcePressure` event sent by a client, and `capt-hook run ResourcePressure` refuses
it on the cold path, so only the host raises the event. The host derives the session's anchor from the
authenticated hook process rather than from the parent pid the request claims.

Escalation sends `SIGKILL` only after the worker recorded its own `SIGTERM` for the same process identity.
It then repeats the full ownership and exclusion checks and revalidates the identity before it signals.
The host runs the escalation stage once per child.

#### Limits

- **The judge sees the daemon's environment.** The model command-line client inherits the daemon worker's
  environment, minus the keys the hooks whitelist. A secret exported into the daemon's own environment is
  visible to it. The judge prompt carries a redacted command line, and the redaction is a best effort.
- **macOS validation and signal are separate calls.** The monitor checks the process, then sends the
  signal with `kill(2)`. In the milliseconds between them the process can exit and its pid be reused,
  `exec` a different program, or change directory. The monitor reads the working directory first and
  the identity last to narrow that window, but it cannot close it.
- **Linux uses `pidfd`.** Signaling through a pidfd rules out pid reuse. An `exec` or a directory change
  after validation can still happen.
- **The worker's last identity check is command text, not the argv vector.** The host tracks a child by its
  pid and sub-second start time at every tick and reads the argv vector it sends fresh at each stage dispatch.
  Right before a signal the worker checks only what `ps` exposes, which is the parent and group ids, the
  whole-second start time, the working directory, and the command text with whitespace collapsed. Two argument
  vectors that join to the same text pass that check, and a process that runs `exec` with such arguments during
  the judge passes with a verdict about its earlier invocation.
- **Other users' processes are not signaled.** The sampler rows carry no user id, and Linux can expose a
  process's CPU use across users. The worker refuses any target whose user id differs from the session's.
- **Disk pressure can be unknown.** On Linux, a process whose `/proc/<pid>/io` the monitor cannot read
  has no disk reading, so only its CPU counts.
- **Children that predate registration are never tracked.** A session registers on its first hook
  event. Anything already running then stays out of scope. Only processes that first appear afterward and
  descend from the session's `claude` process are tracked.
- **Reparented children can drop out.** A process is identified by its pid and start time, so
  reparenting does not make a new identity. A descendant that leaves the session's process subtree is dropped.
  The own children of a child the monitor stopped are tracked only if they first appeared after
  registration and still descend from the session.
- **A calm child keeps its warning.** A child that drops below the thresholds is not warned a second time
  for the same run.
